issues.legal_issue: The urgency power may be exercised for land that is neither waste nor arable when the governing law extends that power to land acquired for qualifying development purposes.
material_facts: The acquired land included houses that were found not to form part of agricultural land.
The land was acquired for planned housing for members of a disadvantaged community.
issues.conclusion: The State was statutorily empowered to exercise the urgency power in relation to this land.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 17(1-A), as amended by the State Legislature, which extended the power to take possession of land other than waste or arable land when acquired for sanitary improvements or planned development. Since the acquisition was for housing as part of planned development, the land's non-agricultural character did not prevent use of the urgency power.

predicates.acquisition_validity_appeal: The proceeding challenges the validity of a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.land_was_not_waste_or_arable: The acquired land was neither waste nor arable land.
predicates.acquisition_was_for_planned_development_: The land was acquired for planned development or sanitary improvement.

issues.definition: When an acquisition challenge concerns land that is neither waste nor arable but is for planned development or sanitary improvement, urgency powers apply to the land.

issues.legal_issue: The Government may dispense with an objection inquiry for urgent housing acquisition when the need for housing remains pressing, notwithstanding administrative delay, unless the urgency decision is vitiated by bad faith or colourable exercise of power.
material_facts: The land was acquired to provide housing for Dalits, whose housing conditions the Court described as deplorable and part of a continuing national problem.
There was delay before and after publication of the acquisition notification, and that delay was before the Government when it invoked urgency and dispensed with the inquiry.
The appellants did not establish that the exercise of power was mala fide.
issues.conclusion: The delay did not invalidate the decision to dispense with the inquiry, and the Court found no ground to interfere with the urgency decision.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 5-A and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the Government must consider not merely whether urgency exists but whether it is necessary to dispense with the inquiry. Its urgency opinion is subjective and receives great weight when supported by material, unless vitiated by mala fides or colourable exercise of power; the court does not sit as an appellate forum. Delay by officials, by itself, does not negate urgency and may make the need more acute. The Court relied on Narayan Govind Gavate v. State of Maharashtra, Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, State of U.P. v. Pista Devi, Deepak Pahwa v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, Jage Ram v. State of Haryana, Rajasthan Housing Board v. Shri Kishan, State of U.P. v. Keshav Prasad Singh, and Kasireddy Papaiah v. Government of A.P.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_dispensing_with_objection_inquiry and government_found_immediate_possession_necessary and housing_need_for_disadvantaged_people_remained_unmet and administrative_delay_occurred and not bad_faith_or_colourable_exercise_established

predicates.appeal_challenges_dispensing_with_object: The proceeding challenges a decision to omit an inquiry into objections to a compulsory acquisition.
predicates.government_found_immediate_possession_ne: The Government formed an opinion that immediate possession was needed.
predicates.housing_need_for_disadvantaged_people_re: The acquisition was intended to address a continuing, unmet need for housing among disadvantaged people.
predicates.administrative_delay_occurred: Officials caused delay before or after publication of the acquisition notification.
predicates.bad_faith_or_colourable_exercise_establi: The challenger established that the urgency power was exercised in bad faith or as a colourable use of power.

issues.definition: Where an inquiry is dispensed with for immediate housing needs that remain unmet, administrative delay alone does not invalidate that decision unless bad faith or colourable exercise is established.

issues.legal_issue: The fundamental right to life and residence encompasses a right to adequate shelter and the facilities needed for a dignified human life.
material_facts: The acquisition was intended to provide housing for Dalits, whom the Court identified as part of a disadvantaged population facing serious housing needs.
The State had undertaken planned housing measures for disadvantaged groups.
issues.conclusion: The right to shelter is a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(e) and a facet of the meaningful right to life under Article 21; it includes adequate living space and necessary civic infrastructure.
issues.legal_principle: The Court read the right to shelter into Articles 19(1)(e) and 21, with the State's duties informed by the Preamble and Articles 39(b) and 46. Shelter means more than a roof: it includes adequate living space, a safe and decent structure, clean surroundings, light, air, water, sanitation, electricity, roads, and other civic amenities, subject to the State's economic resources. The Court relied on P.G. Gupta v. State of Gujarat, Shantistar Builders v. Narayan Khimalal Totame, State of Karnataka v. Narasimhamurthy, Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation, and Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi, as well as Article 25(1) of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Article 11(1) of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.

predicates.state_housing_policy_case: The case concerns State action or policy addressing housing.
predicates.state_was_addressing_their_housing_needs: The State was taking measures to meet those people's housing needs.

issues.definition: When disadvantaged people lack decent shelter and the State is addressing their housing needs, adequate shelter and necessary civic facilities are fundamental rights.

issues.legal_issue: Compulsory acquisition for a public purpose does not violate the owner's right to life merely because it removes land that was the owner's means of livelihood, where acquisition follows lawful procedure and compensation is provided.
material_facts: The appellants claimed that the acquired land was their only source of livelihood.
The land was compulsorily acquired for the public purpose of providing housing.
The acquisition procedure provided for compensation, solatium, and interest.
issues.conclusion: The claim that acquisition deprived the appellants of their right to livelihood under Article 21 was unsustainable.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that, for a public purpose, an individual's ownership right must yield to the public purpose when the State exercises its power of eminent domain according to law. Sections 23, 23(1-A), 28, and 31 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provide for compensation and related recompense. The Court distinguished lawful acquisition from deprivation of livelihood contrary to Article 21 and considered the principles in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation concerning livelihood as part of the right to life.

rule.if: compulsory_acquisition_appeal and owner_lost_land_used_for_livelihood and acquisition_served_a_public_purpose and lawful_procedure_was_followed and compensation_and_related_recompense_were_provided

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_appeal: The proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.owner_lost_land_used_for_livelihood: The owner lost land that was used as a means of livelihood.
predicates.acquisition_served_a_public_purpose: The acquisition served a public purpose.
predicates.lawful_procedure_was_followed: The acquisition was carried out according to the applicable legal procedure.
predicates.compensation_and_related_recompense_were: The acquisition law provided compensation and related recompense for the loss.

issues.definition: When land used for livelihood is acquired for a public purpose through lawful procedure with compensation and related recompense, its loss alone does not violate the right to life.
